---
title: "Internal Migration in Canada"
subtitle: "Push–Pull Factors and the COVID-19 Structural Shift"
---

## Overview

Internal migration — residents moving between and within Canadian provinces — reshapes local labour markets, housing demand, and public-service planning more immediately than international immigration, yet receives far less attention. This project studies CMA-level net internal migration from 2001 to 2024 under two distinct research goals.

[Primary — Prediction (RQ1, RQ2)]{.lead-label} How much variance in CMA net interprovincial and intraprovincial migration rate (per 1,000 residents) can push–pull structural factors explain, and which model family generalises best out of time?

[Secondary — Inference (RQ3)]{.lead-label} Is the 2020–2024 COVID period associated with a structural shift in migration trend, beyond what push–pull conditions alone predict, and does that shift differ by CMA size?

## Findings

#### Prediction

1. Tree models substantially outperform linear models for both migration types. Random Forest reaches holdout R² of 0.42 for intraprovincial rate and 0.30 for interprovincial rate; OLS reaches 0.22 and 0.03 respectively — an order-of-magnitude improvement for the interprovincial model and a meaningful gain for the intraprovincial model.
2. Intraprovincial migration is substantially more predictable than interprovincial migration. Within-province flows track housing affordability and demographic age structure cleanly; cross-provincial flows depend more on shock-driven opportunities (resource booms, pandemic-era relocation) that structural features approximate less well.

#### Inference

3. The COVID structural shift is statistically detectable for interprovincial migration — the year-trend coefficient for large CMAs drops by 0.72 per 1,000 per year post-2020 (HC3 p = 0.04). On the intraprovincial side the linear interaction does not reach significance (p = 0.14), but the GAM partial-effect plot shows a pronounced 2020–2022 dip and partial 2023 rebound that a linear specification cannot capture.
4. International in-migration is a strongly negative predictor of intraprovincial net flows (HC3 p < 10⁻¹⁸): CMAs receiving more international migrants tend to lose residents to other CMAs in the same province, consistent with a displacement mechanism that warrants follow-up work.

## Data

Five Statistics Canada tables, all accessed via the public bulk CSV endpoint (no API key required):

| Table | Content | Geography |
|---|---|---|
| 17-10-0149-01 | Components of population change (net migration outcomes) | CMA |
| 17-10-0148-01 | Population estimates (age structure) | CMA |
| 34-10-0133-01 | CMHC average rents | CMA |
| 14-10-0020-01 | Unemployment and participation rate | Province |
| 27-10-0273-02 | R&D expenditures by performing sector | Province |

After cleaning and merging, the panel contains 40 CMAs × 24 years = **960 CMA-year observations**.
